title: Counting employees: the threshold map
summary: Which state and federal statutes switch on at 1, 3, 5, 15, 20, 25 and 50 employees, and how each one counts.

blocks.text: Most employment statutes apply only above an employee count, and the counts are not harmonized. A North Carolina employer with 18 employees is covered by Title VII and the ADA but not by the ADEA or FMLA; the same employer is covered by the state Workers' Compensation Act and lawful-products statute but not by state E-Verify. Each statute also counts differently: some count heads in the State, some count employees for each working day in 20 or more calendar weeks, some count full-time employees only.

items: Federal counts use a payroll method: an employee counts for each working day the person is on the payroll, whether or not at work, so part-time staff count.

Owners who are also employees, corporate officers and family members may count under one statute and not another; the workers' compensation page of the Industrial Commission states that corporate officers count toward the three-employee threshold.
A count that hovers near a threshold needs to be checked against the prior calendar year as well as the current one, because the federal look-back is the current or preceding year.

blocks.text: The common mistake is using a single headcount from the org chart for every statute. An employer that has 14 full-time and 3 part-time employees has 17 employees under Title VII's payroll method and is covered; the same employer counted only full-time staff, concluded it was under 15, and never adopted a harassment policy or posted the EEOC notice. Build the threshold map per statute and revisit it each January.
This is training, not legal advice.
